title: Inheritance tax rate
headline: 40% above £325,000, frozen since 2009. Abolition costs £13.7bn.
description: Set the rate charged on estates above the £325,000 nil-rate band (frozen since 2009 and now to April 2031): keep it at 40%, move it between 30% and 50%, or abolish the tax. Rises use HMRC's ready reckoner; cuts mirror it; abolition gives up the OBR's whole inheritance tax line (£13.7bn in 2029-30).

baselinePolicy.text: Standard rate 40% above a £325,000 nil-rate band plus a £175,000 residence nil-rate band; thresholds frozen until April 2031 (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 55).
alreadyIncludes: Nil-rate band, residence nil-rate band and the 100% agricultural and business property relief allowance frozen for a further year, to April 2031 (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 55).

level.label: Inheritance tax rate
level.note: The standard rate is 40% on the part of an estate above the nil-rate band.

rows.label: Increase standard rate for estates left on death by 1 percentage point

rawSource.note: HMRC publishes the effect of a 1 percentage point rise only. Rises are that row times the number of points; cuts mirror it (an assumption); abolition is minus the OBR's inheritance tax receipts (EFO Table A.5), so no behavioural response is included for it.

uprating.head: receiptsByTax.inheritanceTax
uprating.note: Shifted to the start year and scaled by the OBR's inheritance tax receipts forecast (Table A.5), so abolition equals the OBR line year by year.

caveats: HMRC's ready reckoner gives the yield of a 1 percentage point rise (£105m, £240m and £290m in 2026-27 to 2028-29). Larger rises are scaled linearly, as HMRC says rate changes broadly are; cuts use the same figure with the sign reversed, which HMRC does not publish and is an assumption here.

Abolition removes the OBR's forecast inheritance tax receipts in full: £11.2bn in 2027-28, £12.8bn in 2028-29, £13.7bn in 2029-30, £14.7bn in 2030-31. It includes no behavioural response, no saving in HMRC administration and no effect on other taxes.

considerations.text: The OBR expects inheritance tax receipts to rise from £9 billion in 2025-26 to £15 billion in 2030-31, driven by rising equity and house prices, a growing proportion of deaths subject to the tax and the October 2024 changes (inherited pensions taxed from April 2027; agricultural and business property reliefs reformed), which account for around 14% of revenue by the end of the forecast and whose behavioural responses the OBR calls particularly uncertain.

HMRC's figure for a rate rise is a direct effect including its standard behavioural assumptions; it excludes wider economic effects. Nothing equivalent exists for a cut or for abolition, which are shown as static arithmetic.

The nil-rate band has been £325,000 since 6 April 2009 and is frozen until 5 April 2031, so more estates pay the tax each year as asset prices rise; changing the rate does nothing about that threshold.
